02.02.2026 01.26.2026 Opens in new window Opens in new window Opens in new window Opens in new window Tech Teamworks acquires Pro Football Focus’ data platform By Joe Lemire 03.30.2026 PFF CEO Cris Collinsworth and the firm’s investors -- including Silver Lake and Western & Southern -- will become shareholders in Teamworks. Kirby Lee/USA TODAY NETWORK Teamworks has strengthened its position in elite football with the acquisition of Pro Football Focus’ enterprise data analytics platform. PFF’s consumer-facing business will remain distinct and will now license the foundational data metrics from Teamworks. Terms of the deal were not disclosed; PFF CEO Cris Collinsworth and the firm’s investors -- including Silver Lake and Western & Southern -- will become shareholders in Teamworks. Collinsworth is now also an advisor to Teamworks. PFF used LionTree Advisors LLC for the transaction. PFF provides football coaches and analysts unique insights and context, such as data labels on when the quarterback threw under pressure, what route the receiver ran and even what stance a pass rusher was in at the time of the snap. PFF is used by all 32 NFL teams and more than 240 NCAA Division I programs. It is Teamworks’ 14th acquisition and 10th in the last three years. Wide Left first reported last month on the prospect of PFF’s acquisition. Teamworks will now vertically integrate PFF data into the platforms of prior acquisitions such as Zelus Analytics , Telemetry Sports and Sportlogiq to better develop predictive models. “Having that PFF data definitely unlocks new possibilities for us,” Karim Kassam, VP/Teamworks Intelligence, told SBJ, noting that the combination of Next Gen Stats in the NFL and Sportlogiq’s computer vision tech at the college level means player tracking data is available at the elite levels of the sport. “The algorithms we use, the AI we use, it can do incredible things,” he added. “But to turn that player movement into insights that can actually be used by coaches and scouts requires football context, requires football knowledge at a very granular level, and PFF brings that uniquely in our space.” Teamworks works with 100% of the NFL, NHL and Premier League across its business units and more than 80% each of MLB, the NBA and MLS. The goal, Kassam said, is to create comprehensive data solutions for coaches and scouts in all sports. Football has been an early priority in the creation of that pipeline. “Having Telemetry and Sportlogiq and Zelus and PFF under the same house really makes data quality a lot easier because, when we get an issue, we’re not at the mercy of someone else to try and fix it or figure out what happened,” Kassam said. additional_source.title: Teamworks Acquires PFF's Enterprise Business, Cementing Position as the Leading AI Platform in American Football
additional_source.article_content: Teamworks announced that it acquired PFF’s enterprise business and framed the move as strengthening its AI platform in American football. The release adds complementary detail to the SBJ report by emphasizing that the acquisition expands Teamworks’ intelligence stack for scouting, recruiting, coaching and roster-building workflows. It highlights executive quotes about pairing PFF’s football context and grading data with Teamworks’ broader data, video and AI capabilities, and positions the transaction as part of a long-term product strategy rather than only a market consolidation move. The release also reinforces that PFF’s consumer business remains separate while the enterprise data operation moves under Teamworks.

market_context_source.title: Teamworks Buys PFF’s Enterprise Unit to Build Dominant AI Platform in American Football
market_context_source.article_content: TipRanks places the acquisition in the wider sports-tech consolidation trend, emphasizing that Teamworks is assembling a multi-layer football intelligence stack spanning tracking, contextual data, workflow tools and predictive analytics. The article is useful as market context because it frames the deal less as a standalone transaction and more as part of a competitive race to own the operating layer for teams’ scouting and performance decisions. It also highlights how integrated proprietary data can create defensibility versus rival analytics and video vendors, especially as AI models become more dependent on exclusive, sport-specific datasets.

02.02.2026 01.26.2026 Opens in new window Opens in new window Opens in new window Opens in new window Tech Whoop raises $575M Series G a $10.1B valuation By Joe Lemire 03.31.2026 Whoop's app has grown beyond a focus on fitness to also included broader wellness features. Courtesy of Whoop Whoop has added $575M in new funding at a $10.1B valuation as it reportedly eyes an IPO. Collaborative Fund led the Series G investment round with participation from more than a dozen institutions, highlighted by medical and pharmaceutical entities Abbott and the Mayo Clinic. Whoop has added a series of new health and medical-grade features and products in recent years, including blood biomarker analysis, an FDA-cleared ECG, insights on a user’s blood pressure and longevity-focused healthspan metrics. Lakers F LeBron James , famously one of Whoop’s first 100 users, invested for the first time along with other superstar athletes who made repeat investments such as Al Nassr F Cristiano Ronaldo and PGA Tour player Rory McIlroy . Whoop, which popularized the concepts of monitoring strain, sleep and recovery, gained attention at the Australian Open when the world’s top tennis players -- Aryna Sabalenka , Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner -- were all asked to remove the device . The app includes one of the industry’s first generative AI coaching tools . Whoop shared that it was cash-flow positive in 2025, its bookings doubled and that it has more than 2.5 million members; users receive the screenless tracking device for free and pay a monthly subscription fee, ranging from $199 to $359 per year. The Boston-based tech company recently announced plans to dramatically expand its staff from 800 employees to 1,400. Whoop founder & CEO Will Ahmed told Bloomberg , “This new raise allows us to really strengthen our balance sheet and ultimately invest more in areas of the business that are already working. We’ve had a very ambitious research and development road map that we’re going to continue to invest behind.” Bloomberg also noted Whoop’s international growth: four years ago, only 30% of users were outside the US, but that is now 60% of new sales. Notably, some of the Series G round investors include the Qatar Investment Authority, Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Investment Company and 2PointZero Group, Australia’s Macquarie Capital and Switzerland’s B-Flexion. title: FactSet Launches AI-Native Banking Solution and Invests in Finster AI
article_content:
FactSet (NYSE: FDS | NASDAQ: FDS), a global financial digital platform and enterprise solutions provider, today announced the alpha launch of FactSet AI for Banking, an AI-powered workflow automation ecosystem. Built in collaboration with Finster AI, FactSet’s AI solution for banking gives investment banking teams and, more broadly, research and sell-side firms, a unified, secure environment that automates complex deal processes and unlocks new data-driven insights. Concurrently, FactSet announced an investment in Finster AI, deepening its strategic commitment to next-generation innovation. This launch marks a bold move by FactSet to reimagine both the established market data and emerging AI agent landscapes, cementing FactSet’s leadership in AI-driven solutions for institutional finance. 
    
    “At FactSet, we envision a future in which powerful intelligence and AI agents seamlessly enhance one another; where, in an ever-evolving landscape, trust in core systems is more essential than ever as clients seek insights at pace,” said Kate Stepp, Chief AI Officer at FactSet. “With FactSet’s new AI solution for banking, we are delivering an agentic ecosystem that unlocks seamless access to an unprecedented array of datasets, proprietary agents, and task automation capabilities, all in direct support of our banking and research clients’ most critical goals.” 
    
    FactSet’s AI solution provides a unified, purpose-built workflow in regulated environments. Through natural language prompts, it orchestrates the production and synthesis of critical transaction assets and other complex processes across the entire deal lifecycle, delivering full traceability. The multiple agents within the solution streamline the proactive, trigger-based generation of pitch materials, company profiles, memos, deep research, and buyer/seller analysis. The solution is available through FactSet Workstation, with seamless integration into Microsoft Office Suite, and supports virtual private cloud or single-tenant deployment to meet the rigorous security requirements of the financial sector.

additional_source.title: FactSet expands agentic AI push in banking with Finster AI partnership
additional_source.article_content: Finextra’s coverage adds industry context on why agentic AI tooling is gaining attention inside investment banking workflows, especially for pitchbooks, diligence materials and internal research synthesis. It complements the original company release by emphasizing regulated-environment deployment, auditability and workflow integration requirements for banks. It also frames the investment in Finster AI as a signal that enterprise financial data providers are competing to own the orchestration layer for AI-assisted deal execution.

market_context_source.title: AI fears temper interest as private equity firms weigh data company deals
market_context_source.article_content: Reuters gives broader market context by showing how AI is reshaping the valuation and strategic positioning of financial-data companies like FactSet. The article notes that buyers and investors are reassessing data providers because generative AI both increases the value of proprietary content and creates competitive risks if traditional terminals lose differentiation. That wider framing is highly relevant to FactSet’s banking launch: the company is not just adding a product, it is responding to an industry-wide power shift in which data ownership, distribution workflows and AI-native interfaces are becoming central to competition against Bloomberg and other enterprise information platforms.

title: PAY360 2026: UK Fintech Shifts from Generative AI Pilots to "Agentic" Deployment
article_content:
PAY360 2026 gathered 6,000+ attendees and 200 speakers at ExCeL London, marking a significant "reality check" for the industry. A core theme was the move from "What can AI do?" to "What are we actually willing to deploy?" Banks and fintechs are no longer just experimenting with chatbots; they are testing agentic AI capable of making autonomous decisions and interacting directly with customers. The tech works, as evidenced by successful trials in the FCA sandbox. 
    
    The conversation highlighted that while the technology gap is closing, a "courage gap" remains among incumbents trying to graft AI onto legacy systems. In contrast, challengers are building AI-native processes from day one. Another critical discussion focused on the use of AI in fraud prevention. With UK fraud losses hitting £629 million in H1 2025, firms are deploying AI to fight increasingly sophisticated scams. However, senior leaders raised concerns about whether defensive AI is being regulated more tightly than the "criminal AI" used by fraudsters to scale eerily convincing scams. The event underscored that the next 12 months will be defined by the willingness of firms to trust their own autonomous technology in real-time financial decision-making.

additional_source.title: PAY360 conference spotlights fraud, regulation and agentic AI in UK payments
additional_source.article_content: Finextra’s report on PAY360 complements The Fintech Times by adding more conference-level industry reaction and a stronger payments angle. It highlights how banks, PSPs and fintechs are balancing AI-led fraud defense against compliance burdens, with speakers stressing governance, explainability and customer trust. The article also reinforces the shift from pilot-stage generative AI to operational agentic systems, providing useful context on adoption barriers such as legacy architecture, accountability and regulatory uncertainty.

market_context_source.title: UK fraud losses hit £629 million as scams grow more sophisticated
market_context_source.article_content: This market-context source is relevant because it explains one of the external pressures driving the PAY360 conversation: escalating fraud losses in UK financial services. By quantifying the scale of the threat and describing how scam techniques are becoming more automated and convincing, the article helps show why banks and payments firms are pushing beyond generative-AI experiments toward more autonomous, real-time defensive systems. It broadens the original story by tying agentic AI adoption to sector economics, regulatory urgency and the arms race between institutional fraud prevention and AI-enabled financial crime.

title: Research Breakthrough: Generative AI Framework for Investment-Banking Risk Management
article_content:
A significant update to a technical framework for generative AI in investment banking was released on March 31, 2026, outlining a structured approach to integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into risk management. The research surveys recent advancements in using generative AI to identify and mitigate financial risks that traditional models often miss, such as qualitative risks embedded in unstructured legal documents and market sentiment shifts. 
    
    The paper introduces a "Multi-Agent Risk Assessment" (MARA) model, which employs specialized AI agents to concurrently analyze market volatility, counterparty credit risk, and regulatory compliance. Unlike previous singular models, this framework uses agentic reasoning to cross-reference data points—such as connecting a CEO's public statement to credit default swap (CDS) pricing anomalies. The updated findings emphasize the necessity of "traceable reasoning," providing human risk officers with a clear audit trail of why the AI flagged a specific transaction. This research moves the state of the art forward by providing a concrete architectural blueprint for "Agentic Risk Management," a shift from passive monitoring to proactive, autonomous risk discovery within complex investment banking portfolios.

additional_source.title: arXiv paper details multi-agent framework for AI-assisted risk management in investment banking
additional_source.article_content: The underlying arXiv research provides the technical basis behind the secondary coverage and adds methodological detail absent from the news-style summary. It describes how multiple specialized agents can divide risk-monitoring tasks across compliance, market and counterparty domains, then reconcile outputs into a traceable recommendation. The paper is useful for newsletter writing because it contributes architecture, limitations and governance considerations, especially around explainability, false positives, supervisory review and the need for human oversight in regulated financial settings.

market_context_source.title: AI fears temper interest as private equity firms weigh data company deals
market_context_source.article_content: Reuters provides useful market context for this research story because it shows how AI is changing the economics and strategic importance of financial data, risk workflows and institutional software more broadly. Even though the original item is academic, the Reuters piece explains the commercial environment into which such risk-management frameworks may be deployed: data providers, investors and buyers are reassessing which firms can turn proprietary financial information into defensible AI-enabled products. That broader lens helps position multi-agent risk systems as part of a larger institutional shift toward AI-native decision infrastructure, not just a standalone technical experiment.

title: Anthropic to sign deal with Australia on AI safety and economic data tracking
article_content: Anthropic said on Wednesday it would sign an agreement to share its economic index data with the Australian government to help track artificial intelligence's effects on jobs and the broader economy. The deal also includes cooperation on AI safety, according to Reuters search results and syndication listings. Australia currently has no specific AI legislation, and the agreement signals a concrete public-sector use of private AI economic-measurement tools for policymaking and labor-market monitoring.

additional_source.title: Anthropic and Australia partner on AI safety and labor-market tracking
additional_source.article_content: The additional report adds national policy context by focusing on how Australian officials intend to use Anthropic’s economic index data to monitor workforce effects and guide future regulation. It complements Reuters with more local economic framing around jobs exposure, sector-by-sector adoption and the absence of dedicated AI legislation. It is useful for writing because it extends the story from a corporate-government agreement into a broader debate about labor-market measurement, public accountability and AI safety governance.

market_context_source.title: Anthropic’s Partners Are Making a Deal With the AI Devil
market_context_source.article_content: Bloomberg Opinion gives broader market context by examining the widening concern that major enterprises and governments are becoming increasingly dependent on a small group of frontier model providers such as Anthropic. That framing is relevant here because the Australia agreement is not just about safety and labor statistics; it also reflects the growing policy influence of AI companies that now supply both infrastructure and economic measurement tools. The piece helps explain the external environment around the Reuters story: concentration of AI capability, strategic partnerships as a route to soft power, and the tension between innovation access and dependency risk for public institutions.

title: California AI order requires firms seeking state contracts to have safeguards against abuse
article_content: California Governor Gavin Newsom signed an executive order requiring companies seeking state contracts to demonstrate safeguards against harmful or abusive uses of artificial intelligence. Based on Reuters reporting surfaced in search results, the measure ties AI governance directly to public procurement, creating an economic compliance standard for vendors that want access to one of the largest state purchasing markets in the U.S. The move has broader implications for AI adoption in public decision-making and for firms selling AI-enabled services to government.

additional_source.title: Governor Newsom issues executive order setting AI safeguards for state procurement
additional_source.article_content: The California governor’s office provides the official policy framing behind the Reuters story. The order adds detail on procurement requirements, agency responsibilities and the standards vendors may need to meet to qualify for state business. This official source is complementary because it helps document the exact compliance expectations and timelines, useful for explaining how AI regulation is increasingly being implemented through purchasing power rather than only through standalone legislation.

market_context_source.title: EU AI Act implementation pushes vendors toward stricter risk controls
market_context_source.article_content: This Reuters market-context source is relevant because it shows California’s procurement order is part of a wider regulatory pattern rather than an isolated state action. Coverage of EU AI Act implementation highlights how vendors are being pushed to formalize documentation, auditing, risk classification and misuse safeguards to keep selling into regulated markets. That broader angle helps explain the competitive implications of California’s move: companies with mature governance programs may gain advantage in public-sector procurement, while smaller or less prepared vendors could face higher compliance costs and slower market access.

title: France's Mistral raises $830 million in debt for AI data centre build-up
article_content: Europe's leading AI provider Mistral has raised $830 million in new debt to buy 13,800 Nvidia chips for a major data centre near Paris, according to Reuters. The financing underscores how AI is reshaping capital allocation, infrastructure investment and industrial policy in Europe. By funding domestic compute capacity rather than relying entirely on foreign cloud providers, the project highlights the economic stakes of sovereign AI infrastructure, including energy demand, supply-chain requirements and the buildup of regional digital-industrial capacity.

additional_source.title: Mistral secures major financing package for French AI compute expansion
additional_source.article_content: Financial Times coverage adds capital-markets and industrial-policy context to the Reuters report, including how lenders and policymakers are viewing sovereign compute as a strategic asset. It complements the original by discussing the debt structure, the rationale for building domestic capacity and the broader European push to reduce dependence on foreign hyperscalers. This extra angle is valuable for newsletter writing because it ties Mistral’s fundraising to AI infrastructure economics, energy usage and Europe’s competitiveness agenda.

market_context_source.title: Europe pushes sovereign AI infrastructure as dependence on US cloud giants grows
market_context_source.article_content: Reuters’ broader reporting on Europe’s sovereign AI infrastructure drive provides strong market context for the Mistral debt raise. It explains that governments and local champions are increasingly concerned that AI value creation could be captured by U.S. hyperscalers that control cloud capacity, model distribution and chip access. That context clarifies why Mistral’s financing matters beyond one company: it sits at the intersection of industrial policy, energy-intensive compute buildout, Nvidia supply dependence and the strategic push to create a regional alternative stack for European AI development.
